tlg0532.summary:
Achilles Tatius (Ἀχιλλεὺς Τάτιος, Achilleus Tatios, 2nd century CE) was, according to the Byzantine Suda, from Alexandria. The Suda's further claims, that he became a Christian and a bishop and wrote on astronomy, are probably later confusions. Papyri show that his novel was being read in Egypt by the late second century CE.

Leucippe and Clitophon (Τὰ κατὰ Λευκίππην καὶ Κλειτοφῶντα, Ta kata Leukippēn kai Kleitophōnta), in eight books, is told in the first person by Clitophon, whom the author meets at Sidon in front of a painting of Europa and the bull. Clitophon falls in love with his cousin Leucippe, elopes with her, and suffers shipwreck, bandits, apparent deaths (Leucippe 'dies' three times), a rival marriage and a trial before the lovers are reunited at Ephesus. The tone is often knowing and comic. The narrator is no model of fidelity, and the novel plays with the conventions that Chariton and Xenophon took seriously.

Achilles Tatius is a writer of the Second Sophistic, and his Greek is polished Attic. He fills the story with learned digressions on love, animals, painting and natural wonders, and with ecphrases (ἔκφρασις, ekphrasis, "description") of works of art. His prose, full of balanced antitheses and short rhythmic clauses, was much admired in Byzantium, although Photius disapproved of its indecency.

timeline.what: Leucippe and Clitophon written (2nd century CE)
Papyri show the novel circulating in Egypt (late 2nd century)
Photius praises the style but condemns the morals of the novel (9th century)
The Suda makes him a Christian and a bishop, probably a later confusion (10th century)
Annibale della Croce's Latin translation of the whole novel
Editio princeps of the Greek text (Heidelberg, Commelinus)

tlg0532.transmission: Leucippe and Clitophon survives in some twenty manuscripts, far more than Chariton or Xenophon, a sign of its popularity in Byzantium. They fall into two main families. Several papyri of the second to fourth centuries, including one that arranges the text in a different order, show that the ancient text was already somewhat fluid.
tlg0532.variants: Editors must choose between the two manuscript families, which differ in many small details. One papyrus places a passage from Book 2 earlier in the story, and scholars debate whether this reflects an earlier version or an error. The date of the novel was once put much later, until the papyri fixed it in the second century.
